# Supporting Information 

## Existing Snow Interception Theories

Parameterisations for predicting unloading of intercepted snow due to snow load and wind speed are shown in @fig-unl-ex-wind.

![The @Hedstrom1998a model of unloading rate with increasing snow load (left, E10) and the @Roesch2001 model of unloading rate with increasing wind speed and canopy snow load (left, R01). Both examples have a constant air temperature of -10°C to disable the influence of warming on unloading and drip.](figs/supplement/figureS1.png){#fig-unl-ex-wind}

Existing unloading relationships associated with air and ice-bulb temperatures are shown in @fig-unl-ex-temp.

![The @Ellis2010 and @Floyd2012b (E10) model of unloading and drip rate (left) and the @Roesch2001 (R01) model of unloading rate (right) with increasing air temperature. Wind speed for the R01 parameterisation was set to zero.](figs/supplement/figureS2.png){#fig-unl-ex-temp}

## Unloading Relationships

Canopy snow unloading measured by the subcanopy weighed snow buckets over all observed unloading events shows some of the melt-driven and dry-snow unloading process emergence. Some diverging process emergence is also illustrated by increased unloading during low wind periods driven by increased canopy snowmelt rates, increased unloading resulting from negative sublimation rates due to the association with melt, and increased unloading with sublimation up until 0.3 mm/hr possibly due to the association with wind speed.  

![Scatter plots showing the mean unloading rate (mm hr^-1^) for differing bins of air temperature (°C), ice-bulb temperature depression (°C), shear stress (N m^-2^), canopy snowmelt (mm hr^-1^), canopy snow sublimation (mm hr^-1^), and wind speed (m s^-1^). Note: unloading was measured by the subcanopy weighed snow buckets, air temperature and wind speed were measured at FT station, canopy snowmelt and sublimation were calculated using CRHM. The canopy snow load corresponds to the midpoint of each bin (0–2, 2–6, 6–20 kg m^-2^).](figs/supplement/figureS3.png){#fig-q-unld-all-bins width=100%}

Statistics testing whether melt and non-melt periods could be treated as originating from the same population, the distributions of air temperature, wind speed, relative humidity, canopy snow unloading, melt, and sublimation were compared between the two periods.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-melt-non-melt-distributions
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing the distributions of air temperature, wind speed, relative humidity, canopy snow unloading, melt, and sublimation between melt and non-melt periods."

melt_non_melt_var_dist_test |> 
  select(-cliff_delta) |> 
  rename(`Median Diff.` = median_diff) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

## Dry Snow Unloading

The correlation between predictor variables was assessed using the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients over the non-canopy snowmelt periods are shown in @fig-non-melt-cor.

![Spearman and Pearson correlations of differing combinations of snow load, shear stress, wind speed, air temperature, ice-bulb temperature depression (air temperature subtracted by ice-bulb temperature), and canopy snow sublimation rate. Pearson correlations are shown in the upper triangle; Spearman correlations in the lower triangle over periods without simulated canopy snowmelt. Bold values indicate |r| > 0.7.](figs/supplement/figureS4.png){#fig-non-melt-cor width=100%}

The full regression statistics and assumption tests over periods without canopy snowmelt are shown in @tbl-dry-snow-reg-full.

::: {.landscape}
```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-dry-snow-reg-full
#| tbl-cap: "Regression statistics for dry snow unloading with various predictor combinations. Coefficients are shown for hourly unloading, derived using ordinary least squares (OLS), non-linear least squares (NLS), and generalised least squares (GLS) regression. Error metrics include mean bias (MB), root-mean-squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination ($R^2$), and index of agreement ($d$). Row names (a) and (b) indicate coefficients, with p(a) and p(b) as their p-values. P-values are not provided for GLS models due to heteroscedasticity violating t-distribution assumptions. The HS row reports the Breusch-Pagan test for homoscedasticity, while the Norm row reports the Shapiro-Wilk test assessing residual normality. Equation variables include: dry snow unloading ($q_{unld}^{dry}$, mm hr^-1^), canopy snow load ($L$, mm), mid canopy shear stress ($\\tau_{mid}$, N m^-2^), mid canopy wind speed ($u_{mid}$, m s^-1^), canopy snow sublimation rate ($q_{subl}^{veg}$ mm hr^-1^), air temperatue ($T_a$, °C), and ice-bulb temperature ($T_i$, °C)."
#| tbl-colwidths: [10, 30, 20, 20, 20]

dry_snow_unld_stats |> 
  filter(!Metric %in% c('Linear/Non-linear Correlation')) |> 
  kable(
    col.names = c("", colnames(dry_snow_unld_stats)[-1]),
    escape = FALSE
  )
```
:::

# Melt Driven Unloading 

![Spearman and Pearson correlations of differing combinations of snow load, shear stress, wind speed, air temperature, ice-bulb temperature depression (air temperature subtracted by ice-bulb temperature), and canopy snowmelt rate. Pearson correlations are shown in the upper triangle; Spearman correlations in the lower triangle over periods with simulated canopy snowmelt. Bold values indicate |r| > 0.7.](figs/supplement/figureS5.png){#fig-non-melt-cor width=100%}

The full regression statistics and assumption test results for periods with canopy snowmelt are shown in @tbl-melt-reg-full.

::: {.landscape}
```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-melt-reg-full
#| tbl-cap: "Regression statistics for melt-induced unloading with various predictor combinations using ordinary least squares (OLS). Coefficients are shown for hourly unloading. Error metrics include mean bias (MB), root-mean-squared error (RMSE), coefficient of determination ($R^2$), and index of agreement ($d$). Row names (a) and (b) indicate coefficients, with p(a) and p(b) as their p-values. The HS row reports the Breusch-Pagan test for homoscedasticity, while the Norm row reports the Shapiro-Wilk test assessing residual normality."
#| tbl-colwidths: [10, 30, 20, 20, 20]


melt_unld_stats |> 
  filter(!Metric %in% c('Linear/Non-linear Correlation')) |> 
   kable(
    col.names = c("", colnames(melt_unld_stats)[-1]),
    escape = FALSE
  )
```
:::
